passage: Every Thursday Pradeep sang in the bhajan circle at the community centre, then helped stack the mats. Tonight Chaitanya pulled him aside by the water cooler. "There's a retreat next weekend with a new teacher. Everyone gives a month's salary to be 'accepted', and doubting is a sin." Pradeep kept his voice mild. "I love the singing and the seva. But I'd want to see where the money goes, and I don't think a good teacher is afraid of questions." He asked Chaitanya to come to the usual circle instead. Chaitanya shrugged, unsure. Pradeep stacked the last mat and went out humming, his faith untouched and his questions still in his pocket.

qa.q: What does Pradeep do at the community centre every Thursday?
qa.a: He sings in the bhajan circle and helps stack the mats.

qa.q: What is Pradeep thinking about the retreat, and what shows it?
qa.a: He is wary of a group that demands a month's salary and calls doubt a sin. His mild voice and his wish to see where the money goes show that he questions without dropping his faith.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do if Chaitanya still decides to go to the retreat?
qa.a: Stay friendly, keep the invitation to the circle open and, if Chaitanya is pressed for money or told to cut off family, encourage talking to a trusted elder. 🙏

qa.q: How might Chaitanya be feeling as Pradeep answers?
qa.a: Chaitanya seems unsure, perhaps wanting to be accepted somewhere but a little shaken by the questions, as the shrug suggests.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps faith, ritual and service but stays discerning about a group demanding money and obedience.

passage: Yogesh reached the temple hall early for the Sunday meal, and the smell of the big kitchen pulled him back to being ten years old, sitting cross-legged beside his grandfather. Aunties called his name and teased him about his beard. Today he had brought a colleague, Dhruv, who followed no faith and stood stiffly by the shoe rack. "Nobody will quiz you," Yogesh said. "Just eat." Soon Dhruv was drying steel plates beside an old man who asked about his work and never about his beliefs. At the door the old man said, "Come again, whenever you like." Dhruv laughed, a little surprised at himself.

qa.q: Who did Yogesh bring to the Sunday meal?
qa.a: Yogesh brought a colleague, Dhruv, who followed no faith.

qa.q: Why might the temple hall matter so much to Yogesh, and what does the smell do for him?
qa.a: It gives him belonging and support from people who know him, and the kitchen smell brings back memories of childhood with his grandfather.

qa.q: How could Yogesh keep the welcome easy for Dhruv in the weeks ahead?
qa.a: Invite him without pressure, never ask him to take part in anything he doesn't want to, and let him decide whether to return.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt at the shoe rack, and why did that change?
qa.a: He probably felt like an outsider and stiff with nerves, but relaxed when he was given a plain task and met with curiosity about his work instead of questions about belief.

grounding: Shows a young man finding meaning and belonging in his faith community while warmly including someone outside it.

passage:
Notes on Eshaan, Wednesday. He came to my desk furious: the accounts team had been told to backdate leave records so that contract staff would lose paid leave they had earned. He wanted to email the whole company that night. I asked him to wait. Over the week he copied the leave sheets, found two colleagues who had seen the same instruction, and filed a written complaint with the HR grievance committee. He knows his manager may freeze his promotion. He is calmer now, not calm. He said, "I'd rather lose the promotion than sign it." I will go with him to the hearing.

Mridul

qa.q: What had the accounts team been told to do with the leave records?
qa.a: They had been told to backdate the leave records so contract staff would lose paid leave they had earned.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's remark about the promotion suggest about what he cares about?
qa.a: It suggests he values acting honestly over advancing, and that his anger has turned into a firm decision, even though he knows it may cost him.

qa.q: Why was gathering the sheets and finding colleagues a stronger move than emailing the whole company?
qa.a: It gave him evidence and allies and sent the concern through a proper channel, which protects him and makes it harder to dismiss.

qa.q: How might the contract staff see Eshaan's complaint?
qa.a: They may feel relief and hope that someone is standing up for them, and perhaps some worry about what happens to Eshaan.

grounding: Shows an employee channelling moral outrage at workplace injustice into evidence, allies and a formal complaint, accepting personal cost.

passage: Naveen found the photo while looking for a charger cable: him and Suraj, sunburnt and grinning on the college trip to Goa, arms around each other. It had been two years since they last spoke properly. He sat on the edge of the bed in his Mumbai flat and typed once: "Found this today 🙂 Hope work is going well. Coffee if you're ever in town, no pressure at all." Suraj replied the next evening. "Haha, what a photo!! New job is crazy, but let's see soon." Naveen read it twice, felt a small pang, then a warm one. He put the photo back in the drawer and texted an old flatmate who lived nearby.

qa.q: Where was the photo taken?
qa.a: The photo was taken on the college trip to Goa.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel after reading Suraj's reply?
qa.a: He felt a small pang first and then a warm feeling, fond of the memory while accepting that things had changed.

qa.q: What could Naveen do next to keep friendships healthy without pressing Suraj?
qa.a: Leave the door open with an occasional friendly message, and give time to friends who live nearby, as he already did. 🙂

qa.q: How might Suraj have seen Naveen's message?
qa.a: Suraj was probably touched but busy with a new job, so the vague reply may reflect a full schedule rather than a rejection.

grounding: Shows a young adult reaching out once to a drifting old friend without pressure and accepting the change with nostalgia.

passage: Okay Hansa, you asked what I do when a stranger asks for money, so here's what happened last week. I'm Santosh, remember, the one who can't say no. I'm coming out of the metro and a young woman says her wallet was stolen and she needs money for a ticket to her sister's place. I felt for her. I also felt that little push of guilt, like if I refuse, I'm heartless. So I said, "Let me pay for the ticket at the counter with you." She said cash only, please. That's when I started doubting. I offered to walk her to the station office or call her sister on my phone. She got annoyed and walked off. I felt bad. But I also felt okay, honestly.

qa.q: What did the young woman say she needed money for?
qa.a: She said she needed money for a ticket to her sister's place.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when she insisted on cash?
qa.a: Santosh began to doubt her story, while still feeling sympathy and a push of guilt. Afterwards Santosh felt bad but also okay.

qa.q: What other safe options could Santosh offer someone in that situation?
qa.a: Santosh could walk with them to the station office, offer to call their family on Santosh's own phone, or pay at the counter directly, and then leave it there.

qa.q: How might the young woman have seen Santosh's offers?
qa.a: If her story was true, she may have found them frustrating, and if it was not, they blocked what she wanted. From the passage there is no way to know which.

grounding: Shows a young adult who helps within safe limits, checks a stranger's story and does not give in to guilt.

passage: Trisha's home bakery in the kasba was three months old when the review popped up, and her cheeks went hot. Deepika had written, "The cake was dry and delivery was an hour late. Sorry, but I'd hoped for better." Under it a stranger had added, "People like her shouldn't cook for others." Trisha sat behind the counter above the cloth shop with her tea going cold. Deepika's review stung, but it was about a cake and a delivery. The other comment was about nothing. She wrote to Deepika: "Thank you for telling me. I'll fix the baking time and your next cake is on me." The stranger's comment she left alone.

qa.q: What two problems did Deepika mention in her review?
qa.a: Deepika said the cake was dry and the delivery was an hour late.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she read the reviews, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt hurt, shown by her hot cheeks and cold tea, but she separated the specific complaint from the insult and answered only the fair one.

qa.q: Why did Trisha reply to one comment and leave the other alone?
qa.a: Deepika's review named real problems she could fix, while the stranger's remark was only an insult and would only lead to trading insults.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel on receiving Trisha's reply?
qa.a: Deepika may feel heard and respected, and might be willing to order again.

grounding: Shows a small-business owner separating valid online criticism from abuse, replying calmly to the first and ignoring the second.

passage: Aditi crouched beside her daughter Ishita, two years old, who was stacking steel bowls on the courtyard mat. "I'm going to the tap for water. Then I come back. Wapas!" She kissed Ishita's hair and walked out in plain sight. Ishita's lip wobbled. "Amma!" she called, twice. Then she looked at the bowls, lifted one and clanged it on the pile. When Aditi returned with the pot, Ishita held up a wobbling tower and grinned.

qa.q: What was Ishita stacking on the mat?
qa.a: Ishita was stacking steel bowls on the courtyard mat.

qa.q: What does Ishita's brief protest and quick return to play suggest she believes about her mother?
qa.a: It suggests she trusts that her mother always comes back: she called "Amma!" only twice, went back to the bowls and greeted her with a grin.

qa.q: What can caregivers do to make goodbyes easier for a toddler?
qa.a: Keep goodbyes short and predictable, say where they are going and use a clear word for coming back, and never sneak out.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel when she sees Ishita playing again on her return?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and reassured that her short, clear goodbyes are working.

grounding: Shows a toddler who has learned her mother always returns, protesting briefly and then resuming play after a clear goodbye.

passage: I'm Jeevan, from the flat below, and I was there when Anirban's mother came back from the shop. He's two and had cried at the door when she left. When she came in with her bag, he didn't run to her. He turned his back, then swatted her leg. She didn't scold. She knelt and said softly, "You got so upset when I left. I'm back now." He stood stiff for a moment, then pushed his face into her shoulder. I can't say for sure what he felt.

qa.q: How old is Anirban?
qa.a: Anirban is two.

qa.q: What might Anirban's turned back and swat suggest he felt while his mother was away, and how sure can we be?
qa.a: They may suggest fear and upset that came out as anger, but the narrator says they cannot be sure what he felt.

qa.q: Why is naming the feeling a better response than punishing the swat?
qa.a: Naming it shows him his need is understood and safe to show, while punishing the anger could teach him to hide it. 🤍

qa.q: What might the swat have been like for Anirban's mother?
qa.a: It may have been a surprise or a small hurt, but she stayed calm and welcoming, which let him come back to her.

grounding: Shows a toddler hitting and turning away on his mother's return, and her calm welcome that names the upset.

passage: Monday. Two-year-old Lokesh cried at the door while his mother, Baljeet, stayed on the phone in the next room. Nobody came. Thursday. He cried again, more softly, then stopped and sat still on the mat. The next Tuesday a neighbour who was visiting found him quiet, not reaching for anyone. The neighbour picked him up, and he went limp against a shoulder. Baljeet watched, then said, "I'll come when he calls. Every time."

qa.q: What did Lokesh do on Thursday?
qa.a: He cried again, more softly, then stopped and sat still on the mat.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have come to expect by the Tuesday, and what cue shows it?
qa.a: He may have come to expect that crying brings nobody, so he went quiet. He did not reach for anyone and went limp when picked up.

qa.q: What should Baljeet do next so Lokesh learns his needs matter?
qa.a: Respond warmly and consistently when he calls, pick him up and comfort him, and ask a child health worker for support if the quietness continues.

qa.q: What might the neighbour have felt on finding Lokesh so still?
qa.a: The neighbour probably felt worried, since the quiet looked like being good but was not, and wanted to comfort him.

grounding: Shows a toddler repeatedly left crying without comfort going quiet and flat, and his mother resolving to respond consistently.

passage: I help in the daycare kitchen, so I watch the door most mornings. Eshaan, two and a half, came on Monday clutching a worn rabbit. Chinmay, the new teacher, sat on the floor a little way off and just said hello. Eshaan's father stayed a while, then said, "I'm going now. I'll be back after lunch," and left. Eshaan cried. Chinmay picked him up, rabbit and all, and hummed. By Wednesday Eshaan walked in holding Chinmay's hand. I can't be sure he felt safe, but he looked it.

qa.q: What did Eshaan bring with him on Monday?
qa.a: Eshaan brought a worn rabbit.

qa.q: How can you tell Eshaan may be starting to feel safe with Chinmay, and how sure is it?
qa.a: By Wednesday he walked in holding Chinmay's hand after being comforted on Monday, but the narrator says they cannot be sure how he felt.

qa.q: What did Eshaan's father do that helped, and why?
qa.a: He stayed a while first, said an honest goodbye with a time for coming back, and let Eshaan bring his rabbit, so leaving felt less sudden.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's father have felt on leaving?
qa.a: He may have felt torn or worried, and comforted to see Chinmay pick Eshaan up so gently. 🙂

grounding: Shows a toddler slowly borrowing safety from a gentle new daycare teacher who greets warmly, comforts and lets the child keep a comfort toy.
